newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian's woes give American astronaut new role.
newsitem.headline: Russian's woes give American astronaut new role.

text.p: His hobbies include theoretical physics and writing computer software, but U.S. astronaut Michael Foale is being asked to perform the mission of his career with just a few tools and loose wires in hand.

Officials at Mission Control outside Moscow on Wednesday said they had asked Foale, 40, to take over for Mir commander Vasily Tsibliyev, 43, who has developed a probably stress-induced heart problem, in repairing the damaged space station.

The repairs, now tentatively planned for the end of next week, are vital to restoring power to Mir, which suffered the worst accident in its 11-year history on June 25 when it collided with its resupply vessel.

NASA has not given the final green light to the British-born Foale's new role, and Russian Mission Control says if he feels unsure in the task, a Russian-French crew now in training and due to dock with Mir on August 7 would take over the mission.
But both sides said they would try a dress rehearsal with Foale and engineer Alexander Lazutkin in spacesuits next Monday to see if they feel happy with a tentative July 24 repair date.

"Our task here is just to judge if technically it's feasible or not, and from everything we've seen it looks feasible," NASA shuttle astronaut Leroy Chiao, who is participating in planning at Mission Control, said in an interview.
"The details we're working on now are the training plan, and we're also looking at the actual EVA (spacesuit operations) procedures and contingency or emergency procedures," he said.

Veteran cosmonaut Sergei Krikalyov, the deputy mission director, said Foale, who holds a doctorate in astrophysics from Cambridge University, was up to the task even though he lacked Tsibliyev's experience in spacesuit missions.
"If I were in Alexander Lazutkin's place, I would go for an EVA with him (Foale)," he told reporters.

During the repairs, Foale would play a supporting role, waiting inside a small airlock which connects Mir's main body with several modules, including the damaged Spektr and the Soyuz escape vessel he was originally expected to man.
Tsibliyev is now expected to take Foale's original place waiting in the Soyuz "lifeboat" in case something goes wrong.
"We probably will simplify the procedure a little bit to minimise crew workload, but it's basically the same," Krikalyov said.

Foale would seal off the airlock area from the rest of Mir and depressurise it before Lazutkin opens the hatch through to Spektr and partially enters the module, which was punctured and is now airless after the accident.
With Lazutkin in the lead, the pair would try to attach 17 cables from Spektr's solar panels to the rest of the ship and then install a new hatch allowing the cables to pass through.
There are several dangers, including the unknown of what lurks inside the Spektr, where no one has been since June 25.

"In normal space flight you restrain everything on the walls so you don't have things floating around, but in the event of a decompression like this it's hard to say what might have come off the walls," Chaio said. "I guess the bottom line is we really don't know what to expect."
Another danger involves the unlikely possibility that the new hatch does not seal the Spektr off from the rest of Mir.
"If there was a huge leak, in the absolute worst case, then the two space-suited cosmonauts would go into the Soyuz and have to abandon ship," Chaio said.
